newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Right unites to blunt retirement-at-55 drive.
newsitem.headline: French Right unites to blunt retirement-at-55 drive.

text.p: France's ruling conservatives united on Monday to reject trade union demands that retirement at 55, conceded to striking truck drivers in December, be extended to other categories of workers.
The issue is shaping up into the next battle between organised labour and the centre-right government, against a background of record 12.7 percent unemployment and severely strained public finances.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe told reporters at a New Year reception that reducing the standard retirement age from 60 to 55 was impossible, and government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said that in the long term, people would have to retire later.
"I am convinced the majority of French people, once it is explained to them, will understand that we can't do it. It's impossible. We must not overburden the economy," Juppe said.
However ministers said the government could consider exceptions for certain physically exhausting professions.

Six public transport trade unions have called a one-day strike for January 24 to demand retirement at 55, a benefit already enjoyed by Paris transit authority staff and SNCF state railway train drivers, who can go at 50.
Juppe said he had flatly rejected a call along these lines by bus drivers in the city of Bordeaux, of which he is mayor, pointing out that they worked a 32-hour week.
"You can't work 32 hours a week and retire at 55...I think this debate is going to be deflated pretty quickly," he said.

President Jacques Chirac, speaking in his political fief of Correze in central France, warned voters on Saturday that reducing the standard retirement age to 55 would fly in the face of international economic reality.

"I hope that our country will not forget the economic and demographic realities of the world we live in...We will not do better if an ever decreasing number of working people have to carry the weight of an increasing number of youths and retired people," he said.
An opinion poll by the BVA institute for the BFM radio station found that 61 percent of French people want the standard retirement age reduced to 55.

Opposition Socialist Party spokesman Francois Hollande said while retirement at 55 might be legitimate for some professions, it was not appropriate for all workers. Priority should be given to cutting working hours to create jobs, he said.

Trade union leaders told reporters they were not seeking across-the-board retirement at 55 but framework agreements that would enable early departures in some industries in exchange for the recruitment of young people.
"This is not about general retirement at 55 but about ways of recruiting young job-seekers," Force Ouvriere leader Marc Blondel told a news conference.
But conservative ministers and senior politicians launched a barrage of arguments against the move, warning that France was in danger of pricing itself out of international competition.

"The question it raises is how we finance this retirement," Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said. "With life expectancy rising constantly...we have to be careful, and I don't believe we can go on indefinitely bringing down the retirement age."

Arthuis said there could be exceptions for particularly exhausting professions, but "it is inconceivable that a great majority of people could enjoy early retirement financed by a minority of the population in work".
Former prime ministers Edouard Balladur and Raymond Barre said early retirement was no panacea.

Balladur, whose government in 1993 pushed through a reform forcing private sector employees to work 40 years instead of 37.5 years for a full pension, said retirement at 55 would aggravate unemployment without creating new jobs. France would eventually have to raise the retirement age, he said.
Trade unions, divided over the importance to give to early retirement, are united in resisting efforts by the CNPF employers' federation to achieve greater flexibility.
